items.content_html: The United Nations warned that drone attacks on commercial vessels are threatening food exports as the Russia-Ukraine war spreads across shipping lanes. From June through October, the U.N. human rights office recorded reports of 164 attacks on commercial vessels around Ukraine’s Odesa and Mykolaiv regions and in the Black Sea; it verified 15 attacks that killed at least 21 vessel workers and injured 43. Recent strikes have also reached the Baltic and waters off Libya, while a maritime risk zone was extended on Nov. 18 toward Romania and Bulgaria. The disruption is raising freight and insurance costs and shifting grain purchases toward European suppliers, but prices are moving unevenly: Euronext’s December wheat contract closed Nov. 23 at €240.25 a tonne, up €3.50, while Constanța bread-wheat and corn quotes fell 1.7% and 1.3%. items.title: [Bambu Lab Community Forum - Latest posts] Auto-detect the failed layer with the nozzle force sensor and resume (A1 / A1M)
items.content_html:
Problem
When filament stops feeding mid-print (clog, tangle, grinding), the printer keeps “printing” in the air. By the time you notice, the nozzle is several mm above the part and hours of printing are wasted. Resuming is possible in principle, but the hardest part is finding the exact layer where it failed. Measuring the part with calipers is slow and error-prone.

Proposal

  1. Add a “Resume from failure” function. With the failed part still on the bed, the printer probes several points on top of it with a cold nozzle, using the force sensor that the A1 series already uses for bed leveling. The slicer knows the model geometry, so it picks the probe points.
  2. From the measured heights the printer determines the last successfully printed layer.
  3. The printer offers: “Print stopped at layer N (Z = X mm). Resume from here?” and continues on the same part.

Optional: detect extrusion loss during printing (force sensor + filament motion data), pause automatically, and offer the same resume, so the part is still in good shape.

Why
It saves long prints and material, and it uses hardware the A1 / A1 mini already have.

Demand

  • The general request “Resume from Layer”: Feature Request: Resume from Layer
  • A community tool that already does manual resume, Layer Rescue: Layer Rescue: resume failed prints from any layer, even after a power loss

People clearly want this. Automatic layer detection would make it safe and easy for everyone.

items.title: [bbc.co.uk] UN climate summit ends without pact as fossil fuel dispute stalls talks
items.content_html: The COP31 United Nations climate summit in Antalya, Türkiye, ended on Nov. 22 without an overarching agreement after nearly 200 countries failed to resolve disputes over fossil fuels and climate finance. The talks ran about two days past their scheduled close, making COP31 the longest COP conference on record. The final draft omitted an explicit reference to fossil fuels, prompting the European Union, the United Kingdom, Panama and vulnerable island states to reject it. The draft referred indirectly to the 2023 COP28 commitment to transition away from fossil fuels but did not spell out a pathway or reaffirm the wording. Oil-producing countries, including Saudi Arabia and Russia, resisted explicit references to fossil fuels, while poorer countries objected that the proposal did not set concrete funding levels for adaptation. COP31 negotiations chair Chris Bowen said fossil fuels and finance were the main obstacles; summit president Murat Kurum said he would not put forward a replacement draft. Countries agreed on separate measures, including a program to support workers and communities through the energy transition and a plan to assess adaptation progress. More than 80 countries backed Türkiye’s proposed goal of raising electricity’s share of global energy use to 35% by 2035, but the goal was not part of an adopted overarching pact. UN climate chief Simon Stiell said he would seek advice on possible reforms to the consensus-based negotiating process. The next summit is scheduled for Addis Ababa.

items.title: [thenews.com.pk] Battlefield use of AI weapons grows as Geneva talks leave rules unsettled
items.content_html: AI-enabled weapons are in use in conflicts in Ukraine, Sudan and the Middle East, while campaigners say armed drones that can independently select and strike targets have appeared in limited cases. The International Committee of the Red Cross says commanders must remain responsible for the lawful use of force. At U.N.-backed talks in Geneva, 128 countries agreed to develop an international instrument on lethal autonomous weapons over the next two years, but left open whether it would be legally binding. Around 100 countries had sought binding rules; the United States, Russia and Israel opposed that push, and the consensus-based forum allowed any member to block stronger language. The process is expected to examine which systems should be prohibited and which could be regulated. Government experts are to recommend the instrument’s form, including whether it should be binding. The International Committee of the Red Cross says commanders must remain responsible for the lawful use of force, including when weapons act with little or no human oversight.

A decades-old theory suggesting that evolution protects its most important genes from mutations has been dealt a major blow. Researchers say earlier studies may have been misled by harmful mutations that disappeared through natural selection before scientists could detect them.

items.title: [time.com] Ebola death toll in Congo exceeds 5,700 as response lags
items.content_html: An Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo has surpassed 11,700 confirmed cases and 5,700 deaths as of Nov. 19, making it the country’s largest and deadliest. Cases have also been reported in Uganda, Kenya and Nigeria. The Bundibugyo strain is driving the outbreak, and no approved vaccine or targeted treatment is available for it. Health workers say early cases can be difficult to identify because initial symptoms resemble those of other illnesses. Late detection, population movement and mistrust of response teams have hindered containment, while attacks on health workers and burial teams have further complicated the response. On Nov. 17, health workers in Butembo, North Kivu, escalated a month-long strike over unpaid wages and bonuses, halting even minimum service at treatment centers.

items.title: [lemonde.fr] Costa’s EU budget draft cuts regional funds for first time
items.content_html: European Council President António Costa’s revised 2028-34 budget proposal would cut EU cohesion funding for the first time, reducing regional development funding by €8 billion compared with the Irish presidency’s previous draft. The change affects a coalition of 17 southern and eastern member states, including Poland, Italy and Spain, that had opposed cuts to cohesion funding. Costa’s proposal also reduces allocations for competitiveness, defence and external action. It leaves direct farm subsidies unchanged from the previous draft, but France says the proposed Common Agricultural Policy funding still fails to guarantee farmers’ income support. The revised framework cuts €204 billion from the European Commission’s original plan. EU leaders will discuss the proposal at a special summit in Brussels on November 26-27. The European Parliament must also approve the eventual budget, and its chief budget negotiator, Siegfried Muresan, has warned that lawmakers may withhold consent over the reductions.

items.title: [cbc.ca] Canadian military to continue howitzer avalanche control at Rogers Pass
items.content_html: Parks Canada and the Canadian Armed Forces have put plans to end Operation Palaci on hold and say there is no set end date for the military’s howitzer-based avalanche-control program at Rogers Pass in southeastern British Columbia. The military will continue supporting the operation while the agencies develop a transition plan. The decision reverses a plan to end military involvement after the current season, when the agreement expires in August 2027. The operation triggers controlled slides above the Trans-Canada Highway to reduce the risk of larger avalanches and also protects a railway through the pass. The Department of National Defence had previously cited changing military priorities and plans to retire older artillery systems as reasons not to renew the agreement.

items.title: [The Guardian Global Development] Ebola killed 46 members of one man’s family. Now he is fighting to save the rest
items.content_html:
Six months after the Bundibugyo strain swept through eastern DR Congo, Sylvain Kabona Tibasima is still trying to warn friends and family about the dangers of the virus

The day Birungi Nembe was born in a hospital in Bunia, in the eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, her mother, Sylvie Bongerize Tibasima, 46, was diagnosed with Ebola. Sylvie died a week later, leaving behind her husband and nine children, including her newborn daughter.

But the little girl had contracted the virus shortly after birth as well. Two weeks later, in early September, her tiny body was placed in a wooden coffin, which was nailed shut and lowered into a small grave by a burial worker dressed in protective gear. Few relatives attended; the risk of infection was just too high.

items.content_html: The U.S. Senate on Nov. 19 voted 51-48 against a measure that would have directed President Donald Trump to withdraw U.S. forces from hostilities with Iran. The resolution, rejected as the U.S.-Israeli war continues, had passed the House in September. A Pentagon official put U.S. war spending at $48.3 billion through Nov. 13, excluding damage to U.S. bases in the Middle East and effects on the global economy. Iran has disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, while Houthi forces in Yemen have targeted Saudi oil infrastructure and ships. Trump said he would defer a decision on any major new strikes until after the start of 2027. Democrats, due to take control of Congress on Jan. 3, have said ending the war will be a priority.
